title: 10. Finding Things
content:
# 10. Finding Things

Never lose a file again. Linux offers two main ways to search: a fast index (`locate`) and a comprehensive crawler (`find`).

## `locate`
Uses a pre-built database index. Instant results, but might be outdated.

```bash
locate my_file
```
*Tip: Run `sudo updatedb` if you just created the file and locate can't find it yet.*

## `find`
The heavy artillery. Search live filesystem based on any criteria.

### Basic Syntax
`find <where> <criteria> <action>`

```bash
# Find by Name (case insensitive)
find . -name "*.jpg"

# Find by Type
find /home -type d   # Directories only
find /home -type f   # Files only

# Find by Size
find . -size +100M   # Files larger than 100MB

# Find by Time
find . -mtime -7     # Modified in last 7 days (less than 7)
find . -mtime +30    # Modified more than 30 days ago
```

### Execution
You can run a command on every file you find.

```bash
# Delete all .tmp files older than 30 days
find /tmp -name "*.tmp" -mtime +30 -exec rm {} \;
# {}: Placeholder for the filename found
# \;: Terminates the command
```

## `which`
Tells you *which* program will run when you type a command. It looks through your `$PATH`.

```bash
which python3
# Output: /usr/bin/python3
```

## Deep Dive: `xargs`
Often paired with `find`, `xargs` takes a list of items and passes them as arguments to another command. It handles spaces and long lists better than `-exec` sometimes.

```bash
find . -name "*.log" | xargs rm
```

## Common Pitfalls
-   **Permission Denied**: `find / ...` tries to look everywhere. You'll get many errors. Redirect errors to cleanup: `find / -name target 2>/dev/null`.

## Practice Challenge
1.  Find all files in `/var/log` that end in `.log`.
2.  Use `which` to see where `ls` is installed.
